subject: clockworkDog
pitch: A wind-up clockwork terrier made of polished brass and copper. Riveted body plates, visible gears turning in its chest, a big winding key on its back, springy jointed legs, floppy leather ears, glass-lens eyes with a green tint, a tail made of a coiled spring, and a little red collar with a brass tag.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure for a clockwork terrier built from primitives in TypeScript—sizing it around 0.45m long facing +Z, and sketching out the material palette with brass, copper, dark leather, and a green glass lens for the eyes.

For the body I'm considering using a scaled sphere or capsule geometry, then layering brass rivet plates on top with small spheres and cylinders as fasteners, and designing a chest "window" made of a copper torus ring with gear-like cylinders and tooth boxes to suggest visible clockwork mechanisms.

Still designing the figure... a winding key on the back made from a cylinder shaft, torus ring, and cross bar; a sculpted head with tapered snout, a dark nose sphere, glowing green glass lens eyes with brass rims, and floppy flattened-sphere ears pivoting from the top of the head; and jointed legs with brass knee spheres and segmented cylinders, possibly using stacked tori to suggest a springy coiled look.

For the tail, I'm working out a coiled spring shape by generating helix points that spiral outward and upward from the rear, then building a tube curve through those points with a copper material to give it that wound-spring look.

Now I'm figuring out the collar with a red leather torus around the neck and a hanging brass tag, then working out body proportions so the legs, hips, and feet line up correctly: setting hip height, upper and lower leg lengths, knee joint positioning, and building the lower leg out of stacked small tori plus a core cylinder to suggest a jointed, spring-like limb.

I'm recalculating body and leg measurements several times to get the proportions right, settling on a body center around y=0.26 with hip joints at 0.19, upper leg length 0.08 to the knee, lower leg 0.09 to the ankle, and small foot spheres near ground level, then checking that the head height clears the shoulder line properly. Now I'm shaping the head as a scaled skull sphere with a tapered cylindrical snout rotated to extend forward.

Still working out eye placement with small lens spheres and brass torus rings facing forward, and positioning the ears as pivoted scaled spheres offset outward and downward from the skull.

For the chest, I'm placing a brass disc window on the front of the body as a flattened cylinder, adjusting head and chest positions to minimize overlap, then adding a copper ring and small gear cylinders with radial teeth boxes inside the window to suggest clockwork machinery.

I'm also adding brass flank plates with rivet spheres at the corners, a copper top plate near the back, and positioning a winding key as a vertical shaft cylinder near the top-back of the body.

Now I'm placing the key's ring (torus rotated into the XZ plane), a cross bar, and a base plate anchoring the shaft, then adjusting the key's height to align with the top plate.

I'm working out leg positions for front and rear, treating the lower legs as spring-like structures made of stacked tori with a central core cylinder, and planning a torus collar around the neck area connecting body to head.

I'm checking the collar torus's size and placement so it doesn't overlap the chest disc — nudging its y and z position and radius since the ring geometry keeps intersecting the disc, and reconsidering whether a plain XY-plane torus is the right shape for a neck collar given the neck's tilt.

I'm also placing a brass tag hanging below the collar's bottom edge, keeping it clear of the head and chest disc, and planning out the small flat cylinder shape and its rotation to face forward, along with noting the shared materials I'll reuse — brass, copper, leather, lens, and red.

For the tail, I'm working out a coiled spring shape rising from the back of the body: I'm computing a direction vector from the base point curving up and backward, then building perpendicular offset vectors so I can spiral points around that direction. I'm planning to feed these spiral points into a tube geometry with enough turns and segments to give it a tight coiled spring look, with a thin tube radius for a wiry appearance.

For the ears, I'm figuring out how to tilt each ear pivot outward and downward using rotation math so the left and right ears flop symmetrically away from the head, solving for the sign of the rotation angle based on which side the ear is on.

Now I'm designing glossy translucent lens eyes with an emissive glow, positioning them on the curved skull surface by solving for the z-depth that keeps them seated within the sphere, and adding small rivet details plus geared mechanisms with brass hubs and a copper ring window on the chest.

Setting up gear geometry, teeth placement, and the import for the Three.js build...

Now I'm defining the terrier builder function with a seeded random generator and a set of brass, copper, leather, and lens materials to give the mechanical dog its distinct metallic and organic surfaces.

I'm sketching the body and head shapes using scaled spheres with brass/copper materials, then starting a gear-building helper that generates toothed discs for the clockwork details.

Now I'm defining the leg structure—hip, upper leg, knee joint, and lower leg segments positioned with cylinders and spheres in brass and copper tones.

I'm working through the finer anatomy: coils around the lower legs, rounded feet positioned to sink slightly below the ground plane, and the tail pivot placement relative to the body's back curve. Then I move to the winding key assembly at the top of the body (base, shaft, and ring loop), followed by the ears, eyes with brass rings and lenses, nose, and snout proportions—checking each against the skull's ellipsoid surface so nothing floats or clips oddly.

Next I'm figuring out the riveted plating—top plate, flank plates with rivets, and a chest disc—nudging positions so they sit flush against the body's curved surface rather than intersecting it. I work out the collar ring's tilt to align with the neck axis between body and head, then place a hanging tag and small link ring in front of it, deciding to skip a canvas-texture engraving on the tag since it's risky to rely on.

Finally I'm constructing the spiral tail using a helical point generator fed into a Catmull-Rom curve and tube geometry, tuning the coil radius, pitch, and turn count so the coils read as a spring without overlapping. I tally up the seven materials needed, confirm the feet clear the ground by only a hair, and get ready to write out the complete object code.
